references.text: Describes the creation of living creatures—sea creatures, birds, and land animals—providing context for the more detailed account of animal creation in Genesis 2:19.
God gives humanity dominion over all animals, expressed through Adam's right to name them.
God forms man from the dust of the ground (adamah), paralleling how animals were also formed from the earth in verse 19.
God's recognition that it is not good for man to be alone—the direct context for bringing the animals to Adam to see if a suitable helper could be found.
The result of naming: Adam gave names to all the animals but found no helper suitable for him.
Man is appointed to rule over everything God has created—animals, birds, and fish—reflecting Adam's authority in naming them.
Adam names Eve, showing a pattern of naming and authority that begins with the naming of the animals in 2:19.
Complementary creation accounts: 1:21 establishes the existence of animals, while 2:19 shows humanity's authority to name them.
Parallel creation account: 1:25 establishes the creation of animals, while 2:19 shows humanity's interaction with them.
Theological connection: Humanity's ability to name (2:19) is an exercise of being created in God's image (1:27).
Command and fulfillment: 1:24 commands the emergence of animals, while 2:19 shows humanity's encounter with them.
Same narrative context: 2:9 and 2:19 both describe God's preparation of Eden before humanity's task.
Narrative continuation: 2:8 places man in the garden, while 2:19 shows man's first action there.
Textual connection: 2:4 is the introduction to the same story of which 2:19 is a part.
Theological parallel: God's naming of elements (1:10) versus humanity's naming of animals (2:19).
Theological parallel: God's naming of time (1:5) versus man's naming of animals (2:19).
Command and fulfillment: 1:20 commands the emergence of animals, while 2:19 shows humanity's encounter with them.
